newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS-Yeltsin to take personal control over budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Yeltsin to take personal control over budget.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, outlining future spending plans during a bitter debate over the 1997 budget, promised on Wednesday to keep future spending under his personal control and ordered a balanced budget for 1999.
But his message to the government, released by the Kremlin, spoke only of a balanced primary 1999 budget which ignores interest payments on Russian debt.
He said the 1998 primary deficit would be equal to 0.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

"That sort of budget can guarantee sustainable economic growth and allow us to get out of the deep crisis in the social sphere," the Kremlin said. "The 1998 budget will be under the president's strict control."

The 1997 budget, with a primary deficit of about 3.5 percent of GDP, has been a persistent headache for the government and ministers faced painful delays in getting the document approved by a parliament dominated by conservatives.
The government deficit figure incluces foreign debt servicing making up 1.5 percent of GDP.
But the budget is already being reworked to take account of a dismal shortfall in government revenues.
Spending will be cut and ministers also plan to raise an extra 34 trillion roubles ($5.9 billion) in revenue.
This includes five trillion roubles to be raised through cash auctions for packages of government shares, and an extra 3.5 trillion through a sale of state property.
Such targets have been missed before -- even 'crown jewel' Russian firms have huge problems and massive debts, and many investors are wary of stepping into the country in a big way.

Figures presented to parliament on Tuesday forecast investment would fall by five percent this year, down from an earlier forecast of a two percent fall but better than the 18 percent slump shown in the figures for last year.
Other figures show an eight percent fall in 1996 investment.
The government also revised down its forecasts for industrial output and GDP and nudged up its 1997 inflation forecast to 11.8-14 percent, from 11.8 percent.

Central Bank Chairman Sergei Dubinin told a banking conference on Wednesday he expected annual inflation to ease to between five and eight percent next year. Russian consumer prices rose 22 percent last year.

Dubinin said the bank aimed for a smooth devaluation of the rouble against the dollar. "The stabilisation of the hard currency rate must take place within the framework of the course we maintained in 1996 and 1997," he said.
The rouble currently trades in a sloping corridor pegged to the dollar with rates calculated to the end of 1997.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said in an interview published on Wednesday that Russian economic reforms had to be deepened and accelerated.
"The government which has been formed is, I believe, capable of coping with this difficult task and is eager to do this work," he told Komsomolskaya Pravda newspaper.
Inflation was falling and consumer price rises were slowing. "There really are changes for the better," he said. ($ = 5775 Russian Roubles)
